lessons.title: Lab: Technical mock interview – core CS

scenes.text: Your first on-campus technical round starts in ten minutes.
Answer aloud, then compare with the model answers.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: Each round gives a question and a timer. Type or speak your answer; the engine checks key points, then shows a model answer and follow-ups. Aim to hit most key points in clear sentences.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Start with a one-line definition, add a concrete example, finish with a trade-off.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reciting definitions without examples.
- Guessing instead of saying 'I would check'.
- Not asking clarifying questions.

rounds.q: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list and when you would choose each.
points: linked list nodes with pointers, O(1) insert at head
rounds.model: An array stores elements contiguously so indexing is O(1) and iteration is cache friendly, but inserting in the middle needs shifting, O(n), and size is fixed in C. A linked list stores nodes with pointers, so inserting or deleting at a known node is O(1), but indexing is O(n) and each node carries pointer overhead. I choose arrays for lookups and dense data, and linked lists when frequent insertions and deletions happen at the ends or at known nodes, such as a queue implementation.
followups: Where is a dynamic array like ArrayList in between?

rounds.q: What is normalisation and why do we do it? Give an example of an anomaly it prevents.
rounds.model: Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once. In 1NF values are atomic; 2NF removes partial dependency on part of a key; 3NF removes transitive dependency. For example, storing the department head in every employee row means changing the head requires updating many rows and risks inconsistency, an update anomaly. Splitting into employee and department tables with a foreign key fixes it.
followups: When would you denormalise on purpose?

rounds.q: Write in words an SQL query to find the second highest salary.
points: subquery or LIMIT OFFSET or DENSE_RANK
rounds.model: I would select the maximum salary that is less than the overall maximum: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp). Alternatively use DISTINCT salary ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1, or DENSE_RANK() = 2 which handles ties explicitly. If there is only one distinct salary the result is NULL, which I would mention.
followups: How do you get the Nth highest?

rounds.q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press Enter?
rounds.model: The browser checks its cache, then resolves the host name via DNS to an IP address. It opens a TCP connection (three-way handshake), negotiates TLS for HTTPS, then sends an HTTP GET. The server returns HTML; the browser parses it, requests CSS, JS and images, builds the DOM and render tree, and paints the page, running JavaScript as it goes.
followups: Where could a CDN fit in?

rounds.q: Explain OOP pillars with one real-world example.
rounds.model: Take a payment system. Encapsulation keeps balance private behind methods. Abstraction exposes a Payment interface with pay(). Inheritance lets CardPayment and UpiPayment extend a common base for shared logic. Polymorphism lets checkout call pay() on any Payment and run the right implementation at runtime.

quiz.q: Best opening of a technical answer?

options: Say what you know and how you would find out

lessons.title: Lab: HR and behavioural mock interview

scenes.text: The HR manager smiles: 'Tell me about yourself.'
STAR keeps stories tight.

steps.title: STAR
steps.body: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Keep Situation and Task to two sentences; spend most time on Action (what *you* did) and Result (a number if possible), then add the learning.

steps.title: Weak vs strong
steps.body: Weak: 'We did a project.' Strong: 'I wrote the issue/return module and tested it with 30 users; time per issue fell from 5 to 1 minute.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'we' for everything.
- Criticising a former teammate.
- Fake stories.

activity.role: Graduate Trainee – HR and behavioural round

points: one or two projects or skills
rounds.model: I completed my BCA with a focus on web development and databases. In my final-year project I built a library management system in Java and MySQL that reduced issue time in our pilot. I enjoy debugging and learning new tools, and this role matches because it lets me work on real products with a team while growing in backend development.
followups: Which part of that project was hardest?

rounds.q: Describe a time you worked in a team and there was disagreement.
rounds.model: In our project two teammates disagreed on using MongoDB or MySQL. I suggested listing our actual needs: transactions for issue and return mattered most. We compared both against that list, chose MySQL, and agreed that the other teammate would own the reporting module. We finished on time and learned to decide using requirements, not preferences.

I used to spend too long perfecting small details and lose time. I now time-box tasks, ship a working version first and refine after feedback. In my last project this helped me deliver the core features two weeks before the deadline.

rounds.q: You are given a technology you have never used and one week to deliver. What do you do?
rounds.model: I would first define the smallest deliverable, read the official quick-start, and build a tiny prototype in the first day. I would ask a mentor about pitfalls, log blockers, and give a short update daily. Learning by building something small reduces risk before the full implementation.
followups: What if you are still stuck on day 3?

rounds.q: Where do you see yourself in three years?
rounds.model: I want to grow into a strong backend developer who can own a module end to end, mentor newer joiners and understand the business behind the product. I plan to deepen cloud and system design skills along the way.
followups: What will you do to get there?

lessons.title: Lab: Scenario round – production problems

scenes.text: An alert fires at 11 PM.
Calm structure beats panic.

steps.title: Framework
steps.body: Clarify → assess impact → check logs/metrics → isolate → fix or escalate → verify → document. Mention communication; stakeholders hate silence.

steps.title: Escalation
steps.body: 'I escalate when the runbook is exhausted or risk of data loss rises.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making many changes at once.
- Skipping communication.
- Not recording root cause.

activity.role: Technical Support / Systems Trainee scenario round

rounds.q: A user says 'the application is slow'. How do you investigate?
points: ask clarifying questions: who, when, which screen
rounds.model: First I clarify: who is affected, since when, which action is slow. I reproduce it and measure response time. Then I check layers in order: client device and network, application server CPU and memory, database slow queries. I change one thing at a time, confirm the fix with the user and record root cause and prevention.
followups: How do you tell if it is the network or the database?

rounds.q: The production database is reported down at 11 PM. What are your first three actions?
points: do not make risky changes alone
rounds.model: I acknowledge the alert, check whether the service is really down and who is impacted. I look at service status and the latest logs for the cause such as disk full or crash. If I cannot resolve quickly I escalate to the on-call DBA following the runbook and update stakeholders. I avoid risky changes without approval.
followups: What would a post-incident review contain?

rounds.q: Explain the difference between a process and a thread.
points: threads share memory within a process
rounds.model: A process has its own address space and resources; threads inside a process share code, heap and files but have their own stack and registers. Thread creation and context switches are cheaper, but shared memory needs synchronisation to avoid race conditions. A browser may run each tab as a process, with threads inside for network and rendering work.

rounds.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
rounds.model: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. TLS encrypts the traffic so eavesdroppers cannot read it, protects integrity against tampering, and the server certificate lets the client verify it is talking to the real site. HTTPS uses port 443 by default instead of 80.
followups: What does a certificate chain show?

rounds.q: How would you secure user passwords in an application you build?
points: salted slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2
rounds.model: I would never store plain passwords. I would hash with a unique salt using a slow algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2, serve everything over HTTPS, rate-limit login attempts and offer multi-factor authentication. I would also avoid logging passwords and use parameterised queries to prevent injection.
followups: Why not use MD5 or plain SHA-256?

tips: Stay calm and escalate when needed

quiz.q: Change how many things at once?

lessons.title: Lab: Menu-driven calculator with switch

scenes.text: Ravi must show a calculator in his BCA lab viva. The examiner types two numbers and an operator and expects the right result.
Ravi decides to read the operator as a char and branch with switch.

steps.title: switch and char input
steps.body:
A `switch` compares one integer-type value (int or char) against `case` constants. Each case should end with `break`, otherwise execution *falls through* into the next case.

In `scanf("%d %d %c", &a, &b, &op)` the space before `%c` is not needed here because the preceding space in the format already skips whitespace.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Input `12 5 *`.

- a=12, b=5, op='*'
- case '*' prints a*b = 60
- `default` handles unknown operators and prevents silent wrong output.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `break` so '+' also runs '-'.
- Using `"+"` (a string) instead of `'+'` (a char) in case labels.
- Dividing by zero without checking b first.

activity.prompt: Read `a b op` (two ints and one char) and print the result of a op b as an integer. Support + - * / (guard division by zero by printing `Error`). Input: `12 5 *` should print 60.
activity.hint: Each case needs a break; check b != 0 for '/'.

quiz.q: What happens if `break` is omitted in a switch case?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
quiz.why: Without break control continues into subsequent cases until a break or the end.

quiz.q: Which case label is correct for the plus operator stored in a char?
quiz.why: Case labels are integer constant expressions; a char literal is valid, a string is not.

quiz.q: What does 7/2 evaluate to when both are int?
quiz.why: Integer division truncates toward zero giving 3.

lessons.title: Lab: Digit sum with loops

scenes.text: Meena's library project needs a checksum feature that adds up the digits of an ID.
She learns that n % 10 gives the last digit and n / 10 removes it.

steps.title: Peeling digits
steps.body:
Repeat while n > 0: add `n % 10` to the total, then set `n = n / 10`. The loop ends after as many iterations as there are digits.

A `while` loop is natural because the number of iterations is not known in advance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing `n = n % 10` instead of `n / 10` (infinite loop or wrong answer).
- Not initialising `sum = 0` (garbage value).
- Using the loop for negative numbers without taking the absolute value.

activity.prompt: Read an integer n (n >= 0) and print the sum of its digits. Input 4825 prints 19.
activity.hint: Use n % 10 for the last digit and n /= 10 to drop it.

quiz.why: The remainder after dividing by 10 is the last digit.

quiz.q: Which loop is best when the iteration count is unknown?
quiz.why: A while loop tests a condition before each iteration, fitting digit extraction.

lessons.title: Lab: Arrays passed to functions

scenes.text: Divya stores four test scores in an array and wants a reusable function for the maximum.
She discovers that arrays decay to pointers when passed, so the length must be passed too.

steps.title: Arrays and functions
steps.body:
When you pass an array, the function receives a pointer to its first element, so `sizeof` inside the function does not give the array length. Always pass `int n` along with the array.

Changes made to elements inside the function affect the caller's array.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Array {4,9,2,7}: max starts at a[0]=4; 9>4 so 9; 2 and 7 do not exceed 9. Sum=22, average=22/4=5.50 — use `(double)sum / n` to avoid integer division.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `sum / n` with ints gives 5, not 5.5.
- Looping to `i <= n` reads one element past the end.
- Initialising max to 0 fails when all values are negative; start with a[0].

activity.prompt: Write `int maxOf(int a[], int n)` and print `max=9 avg=5.50` for the array {4,9,2,7}.
activity.hint: Cast sum to double before dividing; print with %.2f.

quiz.q: Inside a function receiving `int a[]`, what is `a`?
options: A full copy of the array
A pointer to the first element
quiz.why: Array parameters are adjusted to pointers.

quiz.q: Valid loop bounds for n elements?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – topper finder with struct

scenes.text: The department needs a tiny program that finds the topper from student records.

steps.title: Structures
steps.body:
A `struct` groups members of different types: `struct Student { char name[20]; int marks; };`. Access members with `.` on a variable and `->` through a pointer.

An array of structs models a table of records.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Keep `best` index = 0; for i from 1..n-1 if s[i].marks > s[best].marks then best=i. Print s[best].name and marks.

steps.title: Extend it
steps.body: After it works, add a function `average(struct Student s[], int n)` and sort by marks with a simple bubble sort.

activity.prompt: Given three students (Asha 78, Bilal 91, Chen 85) in an array of structs, print the topper as `Bilal 91`.
activity.hint: Track the index of the best student, not just the marks.

quiz.why: Each element is a record like a row.

quiz.why: You need to remember which record is best.

courses.title: Digital Fundamentals and Number Systems
courses.summary: Binary, octal and hexadecimal conversion, Boolean algebra, logic functions and combinational building blocks such as adders and comparators, practised with short Python simulations. Related theory: uni-cse-coa.
outcomes: Learners can convert between decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal
Learners can evaluate Boolean expressions and truth tables

Learners can design a small comparator

lessons.title: Lab: Convert between number systems

scenes.text: Karan sees the hex value 9C in a debugger and wonders what it equals in decimal.
He learns that each hex digit is exactly four bits.

steps.title: Positional systems
steps.body:
A number in base b is a sum of digit × b^position. Binary uses 0/1, octal 0–7, hex 0–9 and A–F.

Grouping: 3 bits = 1 octal digit, 4 bits = 1 hex digit, so conversions between binary and octal/hex are just regrouping.

steps.title: Solved example: 156
steps.body:
Decimal → binary by successive division by 2 gives remainders (reading bottom-up) 10011100.

Group 1001 1100 → hex **9C**. Group 010 011 100 → octal **234**. Check: 9×16+12=156.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading remainders top-down instead of bottom-up.
- Forgetting that hex letters A–F stand for 10–15.
- Dropping leading zeros when grouping from the wrong end; always group from the binary point outward.

activity.prompt: Print the binary, hex and octal forms of 156 (no prefixes, hex in uppercase) on one line separated by spaces.
activity.solution:
n = 156
print(format(n,'b'), format(n,'X'), format(n,'o'))

quiz.q: Each hex digit corresponds to how many bits?

lessons.title: Lab: Boolean algebra and truth tables

scenes.text: Neha's lab alarm should ring when at least two of three door sensors trigger.
She turns the rule into a Boolean function and checks every row.

steps.title: Laws you need
steps.body:
AND (·), OR (+), NOT (′). Key laws: identity, null, idempotent, complement, commutative, associative, distributive, **De Morgan**: (A·B)′ = A′+B′ and (A+B)′ = A′·B′, absorption A+A·B=A.

A truth table with n inputs has 2^n rows.

steps.title: Majority function
steps.body: F = AB + BC + AC. F=1 for rows 011,101,110,111 → four minterms. So 4 of 8 rows output 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying De Morgan but forgetting to flip the operator.
- Treating + as arithmetic addition (1+1=1 in Boolean algebra).
- Missing rows in a truth table; enumerate in binary order.

activity.prompt: Count how many of the 8 input combinations make F = AB + BC + AC equal to 1 and print the count.
activity.hint: Use & for AND and | for OR on 0/1 values.

quiz.why: NOT of an OR is the AND of NOTs.

quiz.q: Rows in a truth table with 4 inputs?

lessons.title: Lab: Ripple-carry adder

scenes.text: Ishaan wants to see how a CPU adds two 4-bit numbers using only gates.
Each full adder takes A, B and carry-in and produces sum and carry-out.

steps.title: Full adder
steps.body:
Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin. Carry-out = AB + Cin(A XOR B).

Chaining four full adders, with each carry-out feeding the next carry-in, gives a 4-bit ripple-carry adder. Delay grows with bit width, which is why fast CPUs use carry-lookahead.

steps.title: Solved example: 1011 + 0110
steps.body: 11 + 6 = 17, which needs 5 bits: **10001**. The final carry-out becomes the 5th bit (overflow for 4-bit unsigned).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the final carry-out.
- Mixing up half adder (no carry-in) and full adder.
- Adding from the left instead of the least-significant bit.

activity.prompt: Implement a full adder with XOR/AND/OR, chain 4 of them to add 0b1011 and 0b0110, and print the 5-bit result as a binary string.
activity.starter:
def full_add(a,b,c):
    # return (sum, carry)
    pass
A=[1,1,0,1]  # LSB first for 1011
B=[0,1,1,0]  # LSB first for 0110
activity.solution:
def full_add(a,b,c):
    s=a^b^c
    co=(a&b)|(c&(a^b))
    return s,co
A=[1,1,0,1]
B=[0,1,1,0]
c=0; out=[]
for a,b in zip(A,B):
    s,c=full_add(a,b,c); out.append(s)
out.append(c)
print(''.join(str(x) for x in reversed(out)))
activity.hint: Process bits LSB first and append the last carry.

quiz.q: Sum output of a full adder is?
quiz.why: Sum is the parity of the three inputs.

quiz.q: Why can a ripple-carry adder be slow?
options: Carry must propagate through each stage
quiz.why: Each stage waits for the previous carry.

quiz.q: 1+1+1 in a full adder gives sum,carry?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – 2-bit magnitude comparator

scenes.text: Zoya's mini-project needs hardware that says whether A is greater than, equal to or less than B.
Before drawing gates, she enumerates all 16 input pairs.

steps.title: Specification first
steps.body:
A 2-bit comparator has inputs A1A0, B1B0 and outputs GT, EQ, LT. EQ = (A1 XNOR B1)·(A0 XNOR B0). GT = A1·B1′ + (A1 XNOR B1)·A0·B0′.

Enumerating the truth table is the safest way to verify the Boolean equations.

steps.title: Counts
steps.body: Of 16 pairs, 4 are equal (A=B), and the remaining 12 split evenly: 6 with A>B and 6 with A<B.

steps.title: Next step
steps.body: Implement the same design with a Karnaugh map to minimise GT; compare gate counts.

activity.prompt: Loop over all 2-bit values of A and B and print the counts of equal, greater and less as `eq gt lt`.
activity.solution:
eq=gt=lt=0
for a in range(4):
    for b in range(4):
        if a==b: eq+=1
        elif a>b: gt+=1
        else: lt+=1
print(eq,gt,lt)
activity.hint: Compare integers directly; 4 values each give 16 pairs.

quiz.q: Number of pairs with A=B for 2-bit inputs?
quiz.why: One equal pair per value, 4 values.

quiz.q: Verification of a combinational design is best done by?
quiz.why: For small inputs exhaustive checking is possible.

lessons.title: Lab: Sets and inclusion–exclusion

scenes.text: A college library has club members: some in Chess, some in Quiz, some in both.
The librarian must report how many distinct members exist.

steps.title: Set operations
steps.body:
Union A∪B, intersection A∩B, difference A−B, complement. |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B|.

For three sets add the triple intersection back: |A∪B∪C| = Σ|A| − Σ|A∩B| + |A∩B∩C|.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Chess 60, Quiz 45, both 20: distinct = 60+45−20 = **85**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding |A| + |B| and double-counting the overlap.
- Confusing subset (⊆) with element-of (∈).
- Forgetting the empty set is a subset of every set.

activity.prompt: With A = even numbers 2..20 and B = multiples of 3 up to 20, print the sorted list of A∩B.
activity.solution:
A=set(range(2,21,2))
B=set(range(3,21,3))
print(sorted(A&B))

lessons.title: Lab: Propositional logic and equivalence

scenes.text: Aditi builds a rules checker for hostel entry and needs to simplify conditions safely.
She proves two rules are equivalent by truth table before refactoring code.

steps.title: Connectives
steps.body:
¬ not, ∧ and, ∨ or, → implies, ↔ iff. p→q is false only when p is true and q false; it equals ¬p∨q.

Contrapositive ¬q→¬p is always equivalent to p→q; the converse q→p is not.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: (p→q) ↔ (¬q→¬p) is true for all four assignments: a tautology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating converse as equivalent.
- Believing a false hypothesis makes an implication false (it makes it true).
- Mixing ∧ precedence over ∨ without brackets.

activity.prompt: Check by brute force whether (p→q) ↔ (¬q→¬p) is a tautology; print True or False. (Define imp(a,b) = (not a) or b.)
activity.hint: Loop over all four (p,q) combinations with all().

quiz.why: Negation turns AND into OR of negations.

lessons.title: Lab: Matrix multiplication by hand and code

scenes.text: Sana's image app swaps image rows and columns using matrices.
She multiplies a matrix by a permutation matrix and watches columns swap.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
An m×n matrix times an n×p matrix gives m×p. Entry (i,j) = Σ_k A[i][k]·B[k][j]. Multiplication is associative but **not commutative**.

Identity matrix I leaves any matrix unchanged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying element-wise.
- Assuming AB = BA.
- Mismatched dimensions: inner sizes must agree.

activity.prompt: Multiply A=[[1,2],[3,4]] by B=[[0,1],[1,0]] using nested loops and print the resulting list of lists.
activity.hint: Three nested loops: i, j, k.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – counting arrangements and teams

scenes.text: A hackathon has 8 registered students; the organiser needs 3-person teams and a ranked top-3 podium.
Selecting a team ignores order; ranking a podium does not.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Permutations nPr = n!/(n−r)! (order matters). Combinations nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!) (order ignored). nCr = nC(n−r).

Product rule: independent choices multiply; sum rule: exclusive choices add.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using permutations when order does not matter.
- Forgetting to divide by r! for combinations.
- Not handling repeated letters in word-arrangement problems.

steps.title: Algorithm

steps.title: Trace `{[()]}`

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Only counting brackets instead of using a stack (fails on `([)]`).
- Popping from an empty list (IndexError).
- Forgetting the final empty-stack test (`((`).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – sort then binary search

steps.title: Two algorithms
steps.body:
Bubble sort: repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs, O(n²). Binary search: compare with the middle, discard half, O(log n); requires a sorted array.

For n=1,000,000 binary search needs at most about 20 comparisons.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: [5,2,9,1] sorts to [1,2,5,9]; searching 9: lo=0,hi=3,mid=1 (2<9) → lo=2, mid=2 (5<9) → lo=3, mid=3 found at index **3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Binary search on unsorted data.
- `mid=(lo+hi)/2` giving a float in Python 3; use //.
- Infinite loop from not moving lo/hi past mid.

activity.prompt: Sort [5,2,9,1] with bubble sort, then binary-search for 9. Print the sorted list and the index separated by a space, e.g. `[1, 2, 5, 9] 3`.
activity.solution:
a=[5,2,9,1]
n=len(a)
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n-1-i):
        if a[j]>a[j+1]: a[j],a[j+1]=a[j+1],a[j]
lo,hi,idx=0,n-1,-1
while lo<=hi:
    mid=(lo+hi)//2
    if a[mid]==9: idx=mid; break
    elif a[mid]<9: lo=mid+1
    else: hi=mid-1
print(a,idx)
activity.hint: Compare a[j] with a[j+1]; use // for mid.

- Ignoring arrival times when they differ.
- Assuming SJF is always implementable (needs burst prediction).

steps.title: Formulas

- Forgetting to subtract 2.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: For one feature: slope m = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)², intercept b = ȳ − m·x̄. Prediction ŷ = m·x + b. Residual = y − ŷ. Fit on training data, judge on unseen data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Extrapolating far beyond the data range.
- Judging a model only on training data.
- Confusing correlation with causation.

m=sum((a-xm)*(b-ym) for a,b in zip(x,y))/sum((a-xm)**2 for a in x)

print(m,b,m*5+b)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not scaling features.
- Even k causing ties.
- Using k=1 on noisy data (overfitting).

- Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
- Swapping precision and recall.
- Forgetting to evaluate on a held-out set.

activity.prompt: Print each member name and number of late loans (returned > due), including members with 0, ordered by name.
activity.solution: SELECT m.name, COUNT(l.id) FROM members m LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.member_id=m.id AND l.returned > l.due GROUP BY m.name ORDER BY m.name;

steps.title: Four-step loop
steps.body: `git init` creates a repository. `git add file` stages changes. `git commit -m 'message'` records a snapshot. `git log --oneline` shows history. Commit small, with messages that say what and why.

steps.title: Message
steps.body: 'Add overdue fine calculation' beats 'changes'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Committing secrets or .env files.
- Huge commits mixing unrelated changes.
- git add . without checking git status.

steps.title: Branching
steps.body: `git switch -c feature` creates a branch. Merge with `git merge feature` from main. Conflicts show markers `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`; edit the file to the correct final content, `git add` it and commit. Short-lived branches and pull requests keep main stable.

steps.title: Conflict
steps.body: Both changed `timeout=30`: pick the agreed value, remove markers, commit.

steps.body:
- Leaving conflict markers in code.
- Long-lived branches.
- Force-pushing shared branches.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – work-rate aptitude drill

scenes.text: The placement written test has 20 questions in 25 minutes; work-rate problems appear in every set.
Use rates: work per day.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Rate = 1/time. Combined rate adds: 1/a + 1/b. Time together = 1/(1/a+1/b) = ab/(a+b). Also practice percentages, ratios, speed-distance and profit-loss; aim for 1 minute per question.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: A in 12 days, B in 24 days: rates 1/12 + 1/24 = 3/24 = 1/8 → **8 days** together.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body: Skip and return; negative marking rewards careful guesses only when two options are eliminated.
